title: Attack by Stratagem
hook: Dust rises from the local-history shelf before Emily turns a rent fight into a better plan.
counterintuition: The cleanest win may happen before the contest begins. If you can change the other side’s plan, you preserve what a direct fight would spend.
tryThisNow: Write the other side’s plan in one sentence. Underline the dependency it needs most, then find one earlier move that makes that dependency unnecessary.
keyTakeaway: Attack the plan behind the resistance before you attack the people carrying it.

breakdown.fastRead:
Dust lifts from the local-history shelf as Emily pulls a footfall counter report from behind the register. The landlord wants a rent increase. A legal fight would drain the bookstore before renewal season. Emily can argue, threaten, and gather signatures, or she can give the landlord a better plan.

She builds a proposal with neighbor petitions, shared events, and traffic numbers that make the whole block more valuable. The rent fight loses its fuel.

The strongest move is often not collision. It is breaking the plan that would make collision necessary.
breakdown.deepRead:
If your plan begins with building mantlets, ask what plan you failed to break earlier. The old siege image is practical, not ornamental: shelters, tools, and mounds take months before the wall even yields. By then, strength has been spent proving a point that might have been avoided upstream.

A fight is rarely one decision; it is timing, proportion, spirit, readiness, and clean authority meeting at once.

David sees that on a half-lit turf pitch after practice. Two coaches are close to signing with a rival academy, and four youth teams would fracture mid-season. He has to decide whether to send a furious parent email or call the rival director first. At 9:05 p.m., he offers a shared tournament bracket that gives the rival academy visibility without poaching staff.

The move works because it attacks the rival plan, not the rival person. Their plan needs coaches, parents, and a public win. The tournament supplies one of those needs without destroying the club David is trying to protect.

Breaking resistance without fighting is not niceness. It is economy.

The five essentials for victory make the same point: know when to fight, how to handle strength, how to unite ranks, how to prepare, and when command is free to act.

This is why the phrase the five essentials for victory matters more as a checklist than as a motto.
breakdown.fullRead:
Rain dots the metal return bin outside Chloe’s library branch. Inside, the after-school tutoring waitlist is three pages long. The council aide who wrote the cut memo thinks the branch is mostly quiet shelves and warm lights. Chloe could rally patrons into a public fight before the hearing. She could also harden the aide’s position by making him defend the memo.

Instead, she brings the waitlist, the branch usage map, and the council agenda to his office two days earlier. The conversation changes from save our library to what happens to these forty-two children after school. The aide still has budget pressure. Now his plan has a hole in it.

The aim is to take the useful thing whole. In a business, that may mean preserving the customer relationship while changing the contract. In a school, it may mean protecting a working program while changing the funding story. In a family, it may mean solving the calendar conflict before it turns into an argument about respect. The more intact the outcome, the less repair work follows the win.

Where is the wall in your current conflict? The wall is the point everyone is preparing to assault: the formal vote, the lawsuit, the public accusation, the resignation threat, the price match. If you are already stacking mantlets and movable shelters, you may be late. Look behind the wall for the plan that made it necessary.

Anders learns this after a cease-and-desist draft lands beside a prototype hinge under a desk lamp. His design firm is two weeks from a trade show, and a competitor has copied the mechanism closely enough to cause trouble. The patent drawing supports a fight. The trade show crate is already packed. It took that legal draft for Anders to see that a licensing conversation earlier would have captured the design intact: fee, credit, and market timing without an injunction.

Force ratios still matter. When you are ten to one, surround. When you are five to one, press. When you are equal, choose carefully. When you are weaker, do not moralize retreat as cowardice. The point is not to avoid every fight. The point is to know which fights protect the object and which ones only satisfy irritation.

Giulia faces a fare war with one red pin on the route map. The competitor has cut fares on a short-haul line where crew overnight costs are already thin. Her first instinct is to match. Then she reads the loyalty data and sees the competitor’s need: they need her to match more than customers need the discount. If she holds price and adds flexibility for business travelers, their low fare burns their own margin alone.

Chidi uses the same logic in a church basement. A rumor page is spreading fear about vaccines. A public rebuttal would feed the post and give it a larger room. Do not fight the post; change the room it feeds on, he tells his clinic team. He recruits church nurses, checks the appointment list, and puts flyer proofs in the hands of people the rumor audience already trusts.

A direct contest can feel honest because everyone sees it. Stratagem can feel suspect because it works earlier and quieter. The ethical test is preservation: are you protecting people, trust, and useful work, or are you hiding harm? Breaking a plan is clean when it prevents waste and keeps the outcome intact.

Win before the wall.

examples.title: Emily offers the block plan

planSpec.domain: bookstore negotiating with a landlord over rent increase
planSpec.stakes: a direct legal fight could drain the store before renewal season
planSpec.requiredBeat: Dust lifts from the local-history shelf as Emily prepares a joint foot-traffic proposal that gives the landlord a better plan than forcing a rent fight.

examples.scenario: Dust lifts from the local-history shelf as Emily pulls the footfall counter report from a drawer behind the register. The lease calendar gives her eleven days before renewal, and neighbor petitions are stacked beside the till. She must decide whether to threaten a legal fight over the rent increase or prepare a joint traffic proposal that gives the landlord a stronger plan for the whole block.
examples.whatToDo: Build the plan that makes the rent fight less useful. Show traffic, neighbor support, and shared events as a better route to value than forcing the store into legal defense.
examples.whyItMatters: The landlord needs higher value, not necessarily a fight. If Emily changes that plan, she protects cash and keeps the bookstore intact.

examples.title: David calls before the poach

planSpec.domain: sports club stopping a rival academy from poaching coaches
planSpec.audience: director of a youth football club
planSpec.stakes: losing two coaches would fracture four teams mid-season
planSpec.requiredBeat: At 9:05 p.m., David calls the rival director with a shared tournament plan before the poaching offer can become a war for staff.

examples.scenario: At 9:05 p.m., David stands on a half-lit artificial turf pitch with coach contracts in his bag and a parent email draft open on his phone. A rival academy is about to offer two coaches better visibility. Before he sends the angry email, David must decide whether to call the rival director with a shared tournament bracket that gives them exposure without taking his staff.
examples.whatToDo: Call before the offer hardens. Give the rival academy a tournament win that satisfies its visibility need while keeping the coaches tied to their current teams.
examples.whyItMatters: The poaching plan depends on visibility, not only on the coaches. Meeting that need upstream can protect four teams without turning staff into spoils.

examples.title: Chloe brings the tutoring waitlist

planSpec.domain: public library facing a budget cut campaign
planSpec.stakes: a public fight over cuts may harden council opposition
planSpec.requiredBeat: Rain dots the return bin while Chloe brings the after-school tutoring waitlist to the council aide who wrote the cut memo, changing the aide's plan before the hearing.

examples.scenario: Rain dots the return bin outside the branch before Chloe locks the side door and walks to city hall. The tutoring waitlist is clipped to a branch usage map, and the council agenda shows the cut hearing next Tuesday. Before the public fight begins, she must choose whether to bring the aide proof that his memo would strand forty-two children after school.
examples.whatToDo: Move the aide before the hearing. Put the waitlist and usage map in front of him while his plan is still a draft, and let the budget story change early.
examples.whyItMatters: A public fight can make the aide defend the cut. Showing the hole in his plan beforehand gives him room to change without losing face.

examples.title: Anders sees the licensing path

planSpec.domain: industrial design firm preventing a patent dispute
planSpec.audience: design director before a trade show
planSpec.stakes: a copied mechanism could trigger injunctions and missed orders
planSpec.requiredBeat: It took one cease-and-desist draft for Anders to learn that a licensing conversation two weeks earlier would have captured the design intact.

examples.scenario: It took one cease-and-desist draft for Anders to see the missed move. A prototype hinge sits under a desk lamp, the trade show crate is sealed, and the patent drawing supports a fight. Two weeks earlier, a licensing term sheet could have captured the copied mechanism intact. Now he must decide what rule to carry into the next design conflict.
examples.whatToDo: Look for the intact capture before legal pressure builds. Offer license, credit, timing, or a joint release while the other side can still accept without public defeat.
examples.whyItMatters: An injunction may protect rights but wreck timing. The earlier licensing move could preserve the design, the show, and the relationship at lower cost.

examples.title: Giulia refuses the fare bait

planSpec.domain: regional airline handling a competitor fare war
planSpec.stakes: matching every fare would destroy margin across the network
planSpec.requiredBeat: What if the competitor needs you to match the fare more than customers need the discount?

examples.scenario: What if the competitor needs you to match the fare more than customers need the discount? Giulia has a route map with one red pin, a fare bucket report, crew overnight costs, and loyalty data on her screen. She has to decide before the noon pricing call whether to match the cut or hold fare while adding flexible changes for the business travelers who actually fill the route.
examples.whatToDo: Do not match the bait. Test the competitor's plan, then answer with a benefit your customers value and their low-price move does not solve.
examples.whyItMatters: If their plan needs your margin to burn too, matching helps them. Holding price while changing the value breaks the plan behind the fare war.

examples.title: Chidi changes the rumor room

planSpec.domain: community health nonprofit facing an anti-vaccine rumor
planSpec.audience: program lead in a city clinic network
planSpec.stakes: a public rebuttal could spread the rumor further
planSpec.requiredBeat: Do not fight the post; change the room it feeds on, Chidi says, then recruits church nurses before the rumor page owns the conversation.

examples.scenario: "Do not fight the post; change the room it feeds on," Chidi says in a church basement where folding chairs face a blank wall. A nurse roster, flyer proof, and clinic appointment list sit on the table. Before the rumor page owns the week, he must decide whether to publish a rebuttal or recruit trusted church nurses to answer questions in the room that already has the audience.
examples.whatToDo: Move the conversation into trusted hands. Recruit the nurses, adjust the flyer, and fill clinic appointments through people the rumor audience already believes.
examples.whyItMatters: A public rebuttal can spread the rumor by giving it a larger stage. Changing the room cuts off the rumor plan without attacking scared people.

questions.prompt: A small supplier is ready to sue a retailer over late payments, but the retailer’s finance team mainly needs proof that deliveries matched purchase orders. What is the better first move?
choices: Send the matching proof and offer a payment schedule before the dispute becomes legal theater.
File suit immediately to show seriousness.
Post publicly about the retailer to pressure them.
questions.explanation: The supplier can break the nonpayment plan by giving finance what it needs to release money. A lawsuit may be necessary later, but it starts a siege before testing the plan behind the resistance.

questions.prompt: A school board member supports cutting a music program because she thinks enrollment is tiny. The principal has data showing it keeps students in school after lunch. What should the principal do before the public vote?
choices: Bring the retention data to the member privately and change the cut logic before the vote.
Wait for the meeting and make the loudest speech possible.
Threaten to mobilize parents against the board member personally.
questions.explanation: The cut plan rests on a false picture of value. Correcting that picture before the vote can preserve the program intact, while a public fight may harden positions.

questions.prompt: A startup wants to match a giant competitor’s discount, even though the competitor has deeper reserves. Which analysis best fits plan-disruption?
choices: Find what customers need that the discount does not answer, then compete there.
Discount harder so customers see confidence.
Avoid the market entirely because the competitor is larger.
questions.explanation: Matching attacks their strength and feeds their plan. Changing the basis of choice lets the startup compete where the discount is weaker.

questions.prompt: A tenant group wants to begin a long court fight over repairs. The landlord is trying to sell the building next month and needs a clean inspection. Which move has the best chance to work first?
choices: Start the lawsuit and prepare for months of discovery.
Ignore repairs until the sale fails on its own.
Bring inspection evidence to the buyer and landlord before closing, making repair the easier path.
questions.explanation: The sale is the dependency in the landlord’s plan. Pressure there may force repair without a drawn-out siege. Ignoring repairs protects nobody.

questions.prompt: A community group plans a protest against a bus route change. The transit agency’s real constraint is driver shortage, not hostility to the neighborhood. What response fits plan-disruption?
choices: Attack the agency’s motives in every flyer.
Offer a route adjustment using fewer driver hours before the hearing.
Demand the old route back without alternatives.
questions.explanation: The agency plan is shaped by driver scarcity. A lower-hour alternative breaks resistance more cleanly than treating the agency as the enemy.

questions.prompt: A manager wants to confront a colleague who keeps blocking a proposal. The colleague’s concern is losing staff to the project. Why might a staffing swap work better than confrontation?
choices: It removes the dependency that made the colleague resist.
It proves the manager is more generous than the colleague.
It avoids all disagreement forever.
questions.explanation: The resistance depends on staffing loss. Solving that dependency changes the plan behind the objection. It is not about looking generous or avoiding future disagreement.

questions.prompt: A city can fight a developer in court over a bad design, or offer faster approval for a revised design that keeps public access. Which question should decide?
choices: Which option humiliates the developer more?
Which option preserves the useful parts of the project while removing the harm?
Which option creates the most headlines?
questions.explanation: The intact outcome matters: housing or investment may still be useful if the harm is removed. Humiliation and headlines spend value without improving the design.

questions.prompt: A team is preparing a months-long internal campaign to defeat a bad policy. They discover the policy owner only needs one compliance concern solved. What should they do?
choices: Keep the campaign because preparation has already begun.
Solve the compliance concern and make the policy unnecessary.
Expand the campaign so leadership feels pressure.
questions.explanation: The compliance concern is the plan’s support beam. Removing it beats building a siege around a policy that may no longer need to exist.

questions.prompt: A negotiator knows her side is weaker and the other party wants a public showdown. What choice fits the source’s force-ratio logic?
choices: Accept the showdown to prove courage.
Withdraw from the direct contest and create a smaller issue where her side has leverage.
Pretend both sides are equal so morale stays high.
questions.explanation: Weaker force should not be moralized into a doomed collision. Moving to a narrower leverage point attacks the plan instead of feeding the opponent’s preferred contest.

reviewCards.front: A conflict is heading toward a formal fight. What should you retrieve first?
reviewCards.back: Find the plan behind the resistance. Ask what the other side needs, fears, or depends on, then look for an earlier move that changes that plan before collision.

reviewCards.front: You are preparing a long legal or public battle. What warning sign should you notice?
reviewCards.back: You may be building mantlets for a siege. Before you commit, ask whether a dependency, alliance, incentive, or false belief can be changed upstream.

reviewCards.front: A larger rival wants you to meet them in their strongest arena. What is the strategic response?
reviewCards.back: Do not feed their preferred contest. Shift the issue to a weak dependency or a customer need their strength does not answer.

reviewCards.front: When is avoiding a fight not avoidance?
reviewCards.back: When the move preserves the useful outcome and removes the need for collision. The aim is not comfort; it is taking the result intact.

reviewCards.front: A public rebuttal would make a rumor more visible. What is the better retrieval move?
reviewCards.back: Change the room that feeds the rumor. Move answers through trusted people and places before the public contest gives the rumor a larger stage.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to attack the plan before attacking the person. The skill is finding the dependency that makes resistance rational, then changing that dependency early enough to preserve value.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a dispute is moving toward formal conflict, then write the other side’s plan and identify the dependency it needs most.
If a colleague blocks your proposal, then ask what resource, status, or risk their objection protects before arguing the proposal again.
If a public fight is forming, then try to correct the decision maker’s plan while it is still a draft.
If a stronger rival invites direct comparison, then shift to a narrower value they cannot easily match.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one expected conflict. Write the other side’s plan in one sentence and name one dependency you can change before the fight becomes public.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, review one argument you had. Ask whether you attacked the person, the decision, or the plan behind the decision. Practice moving one level earlier next time.

memorableLines.text: The strongest move is often not collision.
memorableLines.why: It states the chapter’s reversal in simple terms without making conflict avoidance the goal.

memorableLines.text: Breaking resistance without fighting is not niceness.
memorableLines.why: It keeps the idea sharp and strategic rather than sentimental.
It turns the siege warning into a short command.
